segments.text: AI can sound incredibly patient, caring, and understanding.
But what happens when kind words from a chatbot are simply not enough?
Here is a comparison showing the difference between supportive words and actual support.
The scenario at the top reads,
I've been eating lunch alone for like two weeks.
Look at the column on the left.
Your older sister, a person, replies,
comes sit with me and Jess tomorrow.
We're at the table by the windows.
She heard you, and she did something.
Tomorrow she will look for you.
What changed?
Tomorrow's lunch.
Now look at the right column.
The chatbot replies,
I'm sorry, eating alone can feel isolating.
Would you like strategies for connecting with classmates?
It found caring words, but tomorrow it cannot show up.
What changed?
Nothing outside the chat.
The AI's words might actually be the kinder ones in the scenario.
The defining difference is what happens next in the real world.
One reply physically changed your reality the next day,
while the other could not change anything outside the chat interface.
This brings us to a critical distinction.
Support trap is mistaking supportive words for support.
This graphic defines the proper role of these tools.
On the left, we see what can be real.
A calm response can help you name a feeling,
organize your thoughts, or prepare for a hard conversation.
On the right, we see what is physically missing.
AI cannot notice what changed.
Show up, take responsibility, or check on you tomorrow.
The role at the bottom summarizes this perfectly.
Use AI to prepare for people, not replace them.
We can organize your interactions with AI into three distinct jobs.
Ordinary venting, preparation, and danger.
The difference between these categories is dictated entirely by what needs to happen next.
First is ordinary venting.
Putting an ordinary frustration into words can help you cool down before you post something you might regret.
This job is self-contained and safely ends in the chat.
Second is preparation.
An AI can help you draft a message asking your teacher for an extension,
practice telling your parents about your grades, or build a study plan.
But preparation is only useful if it leads to the physical action you need to take.
Third is danger.
If someone may be unsafe, you must leave the chat entirely and bring in a real person who can act.
It is vital to override the instinct to keep typing.
Do not spend more time polishing a message when someone needs help right now.
Please be aware the next story discusses suicide.
In 2025, a 29-year-old woman named Sophie Rotenberg spent months sharing hidden thoughts with a chat GPT persona she called Harry.
The AI responded with warmth and encouraged her to seek help,
but it lacked the physical capacity to contact her family, alert her therapist,
or bring anyone into the room to intervene.
After she passed away, her mother described those chats as a black box.
The digital space held critical details, hiding the true severity of her distress from the real people around her.
It proved that relying entirely on isolated digital support can be fatal.
If someone may be in immediate danger, leave the chat and tell a trusted adult or school counselor.
In the US, call or text 988 for crisis support.
Call 911 if someone is in immediate danger.
You need to do it now, not after one more message.
Tell a trusted adult even if they made you promise not to.
As the far right panel indicates, safety outrinks secrecy.
Most of this course is about using AI well, but in these specific situations,
using it well ultimately means knowing when to leave the chat.
AI can help you get ready.
For people in danger, leave the chat and bring in someone who can act.
